In April 1507, a small print shop in the Duchy of Lorraine produced something unprecedented: a world map printed on twelve separate sheets, assembled to roughly eight feet by four feet, accompanied by a 103-page cosmographical treatise. It was the work of a young German cartographer and a group of humanist scholars operating under the name Gymnasium Vosagense.
On this map, for the first time in recorded cartographic history, the landmasses of the New World were given a single name — borrowed from the Latinised first name of an Italian merchant-explorer whose published letters had persuaded the mapmakers that these were not the outer edges of Asia, as Columbus had always insisted, but an entirely separate continent. The cartographer later changed his mind about the attribution and on subsequent editions replaced the name with the Latin for "unknown land." But it was far too late. Millions of printed copies had already circulated across literate Europe.
Only one copy of the 1507 edition survived the following centuries, forgotten in a German castle until rediscovery in 1901. In 2003, an American institution purchased it for ten million dollars — the highest price ever paid for a single printed document.
Name the cartographer responsible for this map. And who was the explorer whose first name — not Columbus's — was used to christen the New World upon it?
